shots.title: A link that no longer opens anything
shots.caption: Used, expired and never-existed are three different problems with three different next acts, so the screen says which one it is. This is the third: a link that came through a message cut in half.

shots.title: The Team screen
shots.caption: Who is already here, and who is on their way. The invite card offers two doors: a link for the volunteer whose Google account nobody knows, and an address for the one the church issued.

shots.title: Opening the invite card
shots.caption: A disclosure on a phone and an ordinary card on a laptop. What is promoted on the small screen is the act, at full touch height, above eleven people — an earlier round promoted the form instead and put nobody on the first screen.

shots.title: Naming who a link is for
shots.caption: Required, because a link row has no address to name it — and eight anonymous rows on a Tuesday is how a season roll goes back into a spreadsheet.

shots.title: The link, shown once
shots.caption: Tally keeps only the hash, so this is the only time it can show the link. Copy, Share, or hold up a QR for the person standing beside you.

shots.title: What the link opens
shots.caption: Jo, signed out, on her own phone. The name of the person who invited her and the gathering it is for, before anything asks her for an account — being asked to sign in first is how a volunteer decides a link is phishing, and they are right to.

shots.title: The QR, for the person in the room
shots.caption: Ten minutes, because its whole safety property is that both people are there. A photograph of it taken over somebody’s shoulder is worth nothing by lunchtime.

shots.title: Who is on their way, and what is still to do
shots.caption: A link says when it stops working and offers Extend. An arrival says who spent it. A gathering the redemption could not add them to waits here until somebody resolves it — the only place that fact is ever said.

shots.title: A person, gathered in one place
shots.caption: Role, when they were let in and by whom, the gatherings they are on, the kiosks they paired. The 9:22 rescue is here: Team → Sam → Nursery → Add, on a phone.

shots.title: Ending somebody’s access
shots.caption: The toggle arms rather than writes, and the sentence is computed rather than generic: which gatherings they are on, and whether they are the last person left on any of them. A confirmation that only asked "are you sure" would be answered yes.

shots.title: Tonight’s gatherings, and the ones that are not yours
shots.caption: Locked, not hidden. A counselor at a door at 6:59 who sees an empty screen concludes the app is broken; one who sees a lock and a name knows what to do.

shots.title: A gathering you are not on
shots.caption: Full names, whoever opened Tally today first, and an admin unconditionally — the person the list names may have been on leave since June. Under them, one button, which puts your name on the Add list and never claims to be a queue.

shots.title: The roster, and who is on it
shots.caption: The chip says how many people can work this gathering. The dot beside it says somebody is asking to be added — eight pixels, no word, no target of its own, because a strip above the first row would push every name under a descending thumb.

shots.title: Who’s on, and who is asking
shots.caption: The sheet leads with the ask, because it is the only thing here that is somebody’s to do. Add puts them on; Clear says it was answered — and marks it, so the person who asked can tell that from nobody having looked.
